This is a Khmer translation of a Thai-language original: Whayooathdee, Photpeechon, "Jackfruit (2nd edition)", Nonthaburi Province, Thailand: Agriculture Lover's Printing House, 1988. text:
This closing chapter also covers processed jackfruit products and processing methods as an outlet for fruit that is not sold fresh. The text notes that a large share of a harvested crop's flesh — the source cites a figure on the order of about 80% of the fruit relating to usable flesh/product yield in the context it discusses — can be directed toward processing when fresh-market conditions are unfavorable (oversupply, damaged fruit, fruit that will not survive transport to market in good condition), making processing an important complement to fresh sale rather than a separate, unrelated activity.

The chapter describes small-scale, often household- or cooperative-level, processing activities such as preparing and selling cleaned fruit segments (flesh removed from the rind and core, sold as a ready-to-eat product, illustrated in the source with an image of workers at a covered stall processing whole fruit into cleaned flesh for sale), as well as other traditional preparation and preservation methods referenced in passing in the source, without going into full recipe-level detail. The unripe fruit is also noted (consistent with the general-description chapter) as commonly cooked and eaten as a vegetable dish, which the source treats as a further form of "processing" and market use distinct from ripe-fruit consumption.

The chapter frames processing as a way to add value and reduce post-harvest loss for a highly perishable, bulky fruit, and connects it back to the book's broader theme (introduced in the extending-harvest and marketing chapters) that jackfruit production planning should account for the full chain from flowering timing, through harvest timing, to how and where each fruit will ultimately be sold or used.
